Draw a sample

Source: R/draw.R
draw.Rd

Applies a sampling design to data.

Usage

draw(data, design, seed = NULL, weights = FALSE)

Arguments

data

A data frame. design_reservoir() also accepts a list, a connection, or a zero-argument generator function.

design

A design built by one of the design_simple() family.

seed

Optional seed, applied only for this draw. See "Seeding".

weights

Attach .prob, .weight and .row columns. See "Design weights".

Value

The sampled rows. See "What you get back".

What you get back

A data frame with the same class and the same columns, in the same order, as data. weights = TRUE prepends three columns (see "Design weights"), and some designs qualify it further:

  • design_bootstrap() prepends a .replicate column identifying which replicate each row belongs to, so all replicates come back in one frame. Split them with split(out, out$.replicate) if you need a list. With output = "indices" or "weights" it returns a matrix of row numbers or counts instead, with a column per replicate.

  • design_reservoir() returns a list when data is a list or a stream rather than a data frame, because there is nothing to make a data frame out of. With batches = TRUE it returns the rows sampled from a function's data frames as one data frame.

  • design_simple() and design_spread() with reserve return a list: the main sample, then the reserves, with a leading integer .reserve column that is 0 for the main sample and numbers the reserves 1, 2, ... in the order they are used. With weights = TRUE it follows .row, and .prob is the main sample's probability for every row. use_reserves() turns the list into the sample to estimate from.

Row names of the frame's own, such as the car names of mtcars, stay with their rows. A row drawn more than once, by a design with replace = TRUE or by design_bootstrap(), gets names made unique by make.unique(): "Mazda RX4", then "Mazda RX4.1". The automatic row names 1, 2, ... number the sample's rows afresh, and weights = TRUE records each row's place in data in .row. A tibble has no row names to keep.

Design weights

weights = TRUE prepends three columns: .prob, the probability that the row was included in the sample; .weight, its reciprocal, the number of population units the row stands for; and .row, the row of data it came from. .prob and .weight are what an unbiased estimate needs: a Horvitz-Thompson total is sum(y * .weight).

They come from the design applied to the population, not from the drawn sample, and some designs have no closed form for them. inclusion_prob() documents which, why, and what to do instead.

Two kinds of design are weighted conditional on the clusters the draw selected: design_cluster() with balanced = TRUE, and design_multistage() without size when the rows taken from a cluster depend on which other clusters were selected. With a of A clusters selected and m_i of the N_i rows of cluster i taken, .prob is (a / A) * m_i / N_i, the chance of the cluster being selected times the chance of the row being drawn given these clusters. The total estimated from it is unbiased given the clusters selected, and so over every selection. sample_summary() says when a sample is weighted this way.

Keep .prob as it is: ht_total(), ht_mean() and as_svydesign() refuse a sample whose .prob was changed. Weights adjusted after the draw, for nonresponse say, go in .weight, and as_svydesign() is the way to estimate from them; ht_total() and ht_mean() keep to .prob and warn when .weight no longer matches it.

The sample also carries its design, the frame rows it came from and a copy of the frame as attributes, which is what lets ht_total(), ht_mean(), sample_summary() and as_svydesign() work from the sample alone.

  • The frame is copied when the sample is drawn, every column of it. Later edits to data, including data.table's in-place :=, setorder() and setkey(), do not reach the sample. Each sample holds its own copy, in memory and in every file it is saved to with saveRDS(), so a list of samples from a large frame holds the frame once per sample, and a sample sent to someone sends them the frame, with any personal data in it. compact_sample() keeps only the columns the design reads.

  • Reordering the sample by [, dplyr::arrange() or data.table::setorder() is safe, because each row finds its frame row through .row.

  • Estimate from the whole sample and use by for groups. Row subsets (head(), s[cond, ], dplyr::filter()), rbind() of samples and joins that repeat rows keep the attributes but no longer match the rows that were drawn, and the functions above refuse them. merge(), column selection (s[, cols]), subset() and transform() drop the attributes altogether. Add fieldwork results with add_fieldwork(), which matches them on an id, or with s$col <- value.

  • A CSV or spreadsheet file and a database table keep the rows and the .row column but not the attributes. as_drawn() rebuilds the sample from them, the design and the frame.

weights = TRUE is not available for a design that samples with replacement, or a design_certainty() whose rest does. .prob there is the probability of being selected at least once, but the sample holds duplicates, so sum(y * .weight) over it counts each duplicate at the distinct-unit weight. The total comes out high by a factor of (n / N) / (1 - (1 - 1 / N)^n), which is about 5% at n = N / 10, 15% at n = 0.3 * N, 58% at n = N and more beyond, applied within each stratum of a stratified design. Use replace = FALSE, or the Hansen-Hurwitz form N / n * sum(y), summed over strata as N_h / n_h * sum(y_h) for a stratified design.

Seeding

With a seed, draw() saves the caller's random number state, seeds, draws, and restores the state on exit, so drawing a sample inside a simulation does not shift the simulation's own random number stream. With seed = NULL it draws from the caller's stream and advances it, as any function that draws random numbers does.

A seed is applied with R's default generator, set.seed(seed, kind = "Mersenne-Twister", normal.kind = "Inversion", sample.kind = "Rejection"), whatever generator the session has selected, and the session's generator is restored on exit with its state. A seed therefore draws the same sample after RNGkind("L'Ecuyer-CMRG"), which parallel code often selects, or under sample.kind = "Rounding" as it does in a session left at R's defaults. It must be a whole number from -.Machine$integer.max to .Machine$integer.max. The same holds for the seed of inclusion_prob(), joint_prob() and plot(). Most designs select rows by their position in data, so a seed is sure to draw the same rows again only from a frame with the same rows in the same order.

With weights = TRUE the sample records how it was drawn in its drawn_meta attribute: seed (NULL without one), rng_kind (the generator used, as RNGkind() gives it), version (of drawn), time, frame_rows (the rows of data) and made_by ("draw()", or "as_drawn()" for a sample rebuilt from a file). sample_summary() prints it.

See also

designs for the full list of constructors, inclusion_prob() for the probabilities themselves, and ht_total() to estimate a population total with a standard error.

Examples

df <- data.frame(id = 1:100, site = rep(letters[1:4], each = 25))

draw(df, design_simple(n = 10), seed = 1)
#>    id site
#> 1  68    c
#> 2  39    b
#> 3   1    a
#> 4  34    b
#> 5  87    d
#> 6  43    b
#> 7  14    a
#> 8  82    d
#> 9  59    c
#> 10 51    c

# The same design, reused
by_site <- design_stratified(strata = "site", n = 12)
table(draw(df, by_site, seed = 1)$site)
#> 
#> a b c d 
#> 3 3 3 3 
table(draw(df[1:60, ], by_site, seed = 1)$site)
#> 
#> a b c 
#> 5 5 2 

# With design weights, ready for estimation
df$spend <- seq_len(100)
s <- draw(df, by_site, seed = 1, weights = TRUE)
sum(s$spend * s$.weight)   # estimates sum(df$spend) = 5050
#> [1] 4966.667
